section_summary: This section contains Sino-Korean Peoples’ League petitions alleging Japanese cultural propaganda, resistance to Americanization, divided loyalties, and strategic threats in Hawaii and the wider Pacific. It also includes citizen letters warning of espionage, mapmaking, mineral purchases, Japanese commercial activity, and American sales of war materials, together with newspaper clippings, State and War Department memoranda, and a 1941 espionage cross-reference. The section closes with a lengthy 1935 petition asking Hawaii’s Territorial Legislature to investigate alleged Japanization through schools, religious institutions, cultural organizations, and consular influence.

subfiles.title: Conclusion of petition to Philip C. Jessup concerning Japanese cultural propaganda
subfiles.from: Kilsoo K. Haan, Sino-Korean Peoples’ League
subfiles.to: Philip C. Jessup, American Council, Institute of Pacific Relations
subfiles.about: The concluding pages accuse Japanese cultural organizations and the Institute of Pacific Relations of encouraging Japanization and ask for Korean representation and an investigation.
subfiles.summary: Haan discusses alleged plans to enlist American educators and clergy in Japanese propaganda and assigns a central role to Viscount Ishii. He cites Japanese language-school enrollment, statements by Takie Okumura and Shinryu Umehara, and Yoshi S. Kuno’s account of Japan’s invasion of Korea. The petition argues that the American Council unfairly excludes Koreans and concludes that democracy and Americanism are essential to peace in the Pacific.

subfiles.title: Under Secretary’s acknowledgment routing note
subfiles.from: Office of the Under Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Under Secretary asks Hamilton to arrange whatever acknowledgment he considers appropriate.
subfiles.summary: This brief State Department routing memorandum refers an incoming communication to Mr. Hamilton. It authorizes an acknowledgment at his discretion.

subfiles.title: Letter warning of Pacific danger and enclosing a newspaper article
subfiles.from: Kilsoo K. Haan, Sino-Korean Peoples’ League
subfiles.about: Haan warns that the United States may face Japan alone in a Pacific emergency and encloses a press clipping about his loyalty campaign.
subfiles.summary: Haan argues that potential Anglo-Japanese and Russo-Japanese understandings could endanger the United States. He urges America to remain firm in the Pacific and asks for sympathetic understanding of the Korean cause. The letter notes that he is touring cities to promote Americanism and organization among Korean Americans.

subfiles.title: American Orientals Urged to Be Loyal
subfiles.about: The clipping reports Kilsoo K. Haan’s call for Asian Americans to demonstrate loyalty to the United States and for stronger Americanism in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: Haan announces plans to organize an American-Korean Citizens’ Club in Seattle and says Korean Americans should participate more fully in civic life. He criticizes Japanese government support for Japanese-American students in Hawaii and cites Laura Thompson’s report that Guam residents desired American fortification. A separate item reports Finnish foreign minister Eljas Erkko’s appeal for neutrality.

subfiles.title: Letter to Stephen Early on U.S.–Japan trade and Pacific security
subfiles.from: Kilsoo K. Haan, Sino-Korean Peoples’ League
subfiles.to: Stephen Early, secretary to President Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Haan argues that agreements with Japan are unreliable without the emperor’s signature and that American trade is strengthening a future Pacific adversary.
subfiles.summary: Haan describes Japan’s military establishment as independent of ordinary cabinet control and warns against trusting Foreign Office assurances. He claims American exports and investment sustain Japanese warfare while forcing the United States to spend heavily on Pacific defenses. The letter discusses neutrality, possible Japanese resale of supplies to Germany, Japanese and Soviet power, and earlier American financial support for Japan. It concludes that American influence is necessary to preserve democratic ideals in the Pacific.

subfiles.title: Petition to Philip C. Jessup on the Institute of Pacific Relations
subfiles.from: Kilsoo K. Haan, Sino-Korean Peoples’ League
subfiles.to: Philip C. Jessup, Institute of Pacific Relations
subfiles.about: The League asks the American Council to investigate policies allegedly assisting Japanese propaganda and Japanization in Hawaii and the continental United States.
subfiles.summary: The petition alleges that Inazo Nitobe’s study of American public opinion encouraged Japanese aggression and that Japanese cultural agencies planned systematic influence through textbooks, schools, universities, and churches. It discusses Setsuichi Aoki, Kanekazu Okada, Ernest O. Hauser, and Viscount Ishii, and reproduces claims about Japanese language schools and divided loyalty in Hawaii. Haan also condemns the Institute’s exclusion of Korean representatives. The petition ends by appealing to American democratic principles and asking Jessup to redirect the organization’s attention from Tokyo to Washington.

subfiles.title: Citizen letter alleging long-standing Japanese espionage
subfiles.to: To Whom It May Concern, Department of State
subfiles.about: Leason asserts that Japanese espionage on the Pacific Coast has operated openly for decades and calls for investigation of commercial networks.
subfiles.summary: The writer says press reports understate espionage that ordinary residents have recognized for twenty-nine years. He alleges systematic activity among fleets, industries, merchants, and produce dealers. He warns that superficial friendship between nations obscures preparations for an approaching break.

subfiles.title: Handwritten warning about Japanese offices, mapping, and conduct in China
subfiles.about: An unidentified correspondent reports suspected Japanese intelligence offices and personnel in American cities and condemns Japan’s conduct in China.
subfiles.summary: The poorly legible letter refers to Japanese headquarters or business offices, the Equitable Trust, New York, Washington, California, and Seattle. It alleges that Japanese personnel are engaged in information gathering and strategic mapping. A postscript invokes Japan’s invasion of China, civilian deaths, sexual violence, and the claim that Japanese promises cannot be trusted.

subfiles.title: Letter to President Roosevelt about suspected mapmaking around Long Island
subfiles.about: The writer reports men with large cameras allegedly making maps around Long Island and strategic New York waterways.
subfiles.summary: Petty recalls an article about men taking photographs from cars and says they claimed to be making maps. The letter lists Long Island, Jamaica, Queens, Long Island Sound, Long Island City, the Palisades, and waterways around New York as areas of concern. It urges vigilance near the fleet and the 1939–1940 World’s Fair.

subfiles.title: Letter reporting Japanese attempts to purchase strategic ores
subfiles.about: Philip reports contacts with a Japanese mining engineer and firms allegedly seeking light metals and other mineral deposits in the Pacific Northwest.
subfiles.summary: Philip says a Japanese engineer admitted that Japan depended heavily on American scrap iron and oil for its war in China. The Japanese consulate allegedly identified three Seattle trading companies interested in minerals, while Portland financiers appeared connected with further sales. Philip also claims Japanese truck farmers occupy strategic locations from British Columbia to Los Angeles from which transportation routes could be disrupted. The letter presents these observations as a warning about the defense of the western United States.

subfiles.title: Letter alleging Japanese responsibility for the Hawaii Clipper disappearance
subfiles.about: Ritter speculates that Japan was responsible for the Hawaii Clipper’s disappearance and urges more intelligence personnel in coastal and aviation areas.
subfiles.summary: The writer connects the missing aircraft and passenger Warren Choy’s reported money with alleged Japanese espionage. He calls for more secret-service and intelligence officers in Atlantic and Pacific port towns and along transoceanic flying routes. He also accuses Japanese interests of stealing salmon in Alaska and offers to serve despite being a WPA worker.

subfiles.title: Opening of letter to Cordell Hull enclosing press clippings
subfiles.about: Ritter criticizes the contradiction between American protests against Japan and continued American sales of military supplies.
subfiles.summary: Ritter asks Hull to read enclosed newspaper clippings. He compares selling arms to Japan while protesting its violence with handing a gun to a shooter and then objecting to the shooting. The argument continues after the enclosed clippings.

subfiles.title: Clippings on American aid to Japanese bombing and Italian criticism
subfiles.from: The Christian Science Monitor and unidentified newspapers
subfiles.about: The clippings criticize American sales of aircraft, oil, scrap metal, and streetcar metal to Japan while civilians in China were being bombed.
subfiles.summary: Virginio Gayda cites State Department figures for American sales of bombing planes to Japan, while Dr. Yu urges a policy of nonparticipation in aggression. Editorial material argues that protests alone cannot protect Chinese civilians. Another article reports that old Danville streetcars were being shipped through Norfolk as metal for Japanese war production, while Italian papers answer Hull’s humanitarian criticism by pointing to violence within the United States.

subfiles.title: Conclusion of Ritter letter urging an embargo on belligerents
subfiles.about: Ritter concludes that the United States should stop buying from or selling war materials to Japan and other belligerents.
subfiles.summary: Ritter says ending commerce with Japan would accomplish more than diplomatic protests. He argues that the United States should set an example for other countries by refusing trade with nations at war. Images of Japanese warfare and Chinese casualties, he says, make his blood boil.

subfiles.title: Letter protesting Japanese-made American flags and warning of strategic vulnerability
subfiles.about: The writer protests the manufacture of American flags in Japan and describes Japanese travel and observation along the California coast as a warning sign.
subfiles.summary: The letter calls it outrageous for American flags and Washington souvenirs to be made in Japan. The writer recounts a journey from Lake Elsinore toward San Diego and says Japanese passengers showed interest in mountains and coastal heights. She warns that such knowledge could assist bombing and urges heavy protection of the Panama Canal. The letter closes with a refusal to buy Japanese-made goods.

subfiles.title: Japan Makes Capital of Our Capital
subfiles.about: The clipping illustrates Japanese-made Washington souvenirs as part of a campaign against cheaply manufactured imports.
subfiles.summary: The illustrated item concerns American patriotic souvenirs manufactured in Japan. Its caption mentions a garbed replica and a Washington Monument ashtray. It was enclosed to support the correspondent’s protest against Japanese-made American symbols.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Lieutenant Commander Itaru Tachibana
subfiles.about: The sheet cross-references a report that Japanese Lieutenant Commander Itaru Tachibana left the United States after an espionage charge.
subfiles.summary: The note says Tachibana was ordered to leave by the United States government after being charged with espionage. It records that he was among the passengers aboard the Nitta Maru. The underlying item was a Washington Evening Star report filed under 862.20218/226.

subfiles.title: Memorandum evaluating the Sino-Korean petition
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes and dismisses as overly general a petition requesting investigation of Japanization in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: The State Department notes that representatives of the Sino-Korean Peoples’ League asked Hawaii’s Territorial Legislature to investigate Japanese resistance to Americanization among the second generation. The reviewer characterizes the petition as incoherent and its charges as too general to be of much interest.

subfiles.title: Military intelligence transmittal of the Hawaii Japanization petition
subfiles.from: James I. Muir, Assistant Chief of Staff for Military Intelligence, Hawaiian Department
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, War Department
subfiles.about: Muir forwards copies of a Sino-Korean petition and connects it with earlier intelligence correspondence concerning Kilsoo Haan.
subfiles.summary: Muir identifies the petitioner W. K. Lyhan as Kilsoo Haan and refers to earlier secret correspondence about espionage groups in Hawaii. He reports that the petition was presented to both houses of the Hawaiian Legislature on March 27, 1935. The Senate referred it to the Committee on Education, while the House had not yet acted. Muir promises reports on any significant developments.

subfiles.title: Petition for a legislative investigation of Japanization activities in Hawaii
subfiles.from: W. K. Lyhan, representative of the Sino-Korean Peoples’ League in Hawaii
subfiles.to: Senate and House of Representatives, Territorial Legislature of Hawaii
subfiles.about: The League asks the Hawaiian Legislature to investigate alleged Japanese cultural, educational, religious, consular, and political influence over residents of Japanese ancestry.
subfiles.summary: The petition alleges that Japanese ministries and the Society for International Cultural Relations planned to supply Hawaii’s schools with textbooks, teacher references, and visual materials designed to improve Japan’s image. It cites Japanese cultural officials, advisers, Hawaii educators, Japanese language schools, Buddhist institutions, scholarship organizations, dual citizenship, consular registration, and resistance to Americanization as parts of a coordinated Japanization program. It also reviews Japan’s strategic expansion from Korea and Manchuria to Pacific islands and warns that Guam, Hawaii, the Philippines, California, and the Panama Canal could become vulnerable. Invoking Washington and Jefferson, the petition asks for a legislative inquiry while professing loyalty to American ideals and support for constructive Americanization in Hawaii.
